The decisive citation is Sir Hugh Evans’s line:

> “I have a book, and it is a good book, and I have a Genesis, and it is a good Genesis.”

I believe this occurs in **_The Merry Wives of Windsor_, Act I, Scene 1**—not Act III, Scene 1, and not Act I, Scene 2. If colleagues can verify the exact scene/line, that would help, but the book-title mention itself is the key point.

This is not the same as the “genitive case” joke in _Merry Wives_ Act IV, Scene 1. That is a grammatical term; here “Genesis” is explicitly named as a book. Since **Genesis** is the first book of the Bible in canonical order, it defeats the otherwise genuine **Numbers** citation in _Henry V_ (Act I, Scene 2), as well as later references to Deuteronomy, Job, etc.

So my current position is: **Genesis, in _The Merry Wives of Windsor_**. The Numbers/Henry V answer is strong only if the Genesis line is not genuine; I think it is genuine, so the earlier canonical book wins.
